title: Disc Brakes
summary: A disc brake slows the wheel by squeezing pads onto a spinning iron disc. Follow one stop from the pedal to the pads, see how a small push becomes tonnes of clamp, and watch the car’s movement energy turn into heat.
learningObjectives: Name the parts of a disc brake and say what each one does
Explain how a floating caliper clamps both pads with a single piston
Follow the chain from pedal force to brake torque to tyre force
Explain why braking is limited by tyre grip, not by the brakes
Show that a stop turns the car’s kinetic energy into heat, and estimate the disc’s temperature rise
beginnerExplanation:
Every car brake does the same job: it turns the car’s movement energy into heat. A disc brake does it with an iron disc that spins with the wheel and a clamp, called a caliper, that straddles the edge of the disc. Inside the caliper are two brake pads, one on each side of the disc.

When you press the pedal, brake fluid pushes a piston in the caliper. The piston presses the inner pad onto the disc, and the caliper body slides the other way to pull the outer pad on too. The pads rub on the disc, and that rubbing slows the wheel.

The brake slows the wheel, but it is the tyre’s grip on the road that slows the car. Brake harder than the tyre can grip and the wheel stops turning while the car keeps sliding — which is why cars have anti-lock brakes.

All the energy of a moving car has to go somewhere. In a stop it becomes heat, mostly in the disc. One firm stop from motorway speed can warm a disc by tens of degrees; repeated hard stops can heat it by hundreds. That is why discs are made of heavy iron and often have cooling vanes between two plates.
technicalExplanation:
Force at the wheel follows a chain of multiplications. The pedal is a lever (pedal ratio i_p ≈ 3–4), the servo adds assistance (gain ≈ 2–5), and the master-cylinder piston turns force into pressure, p = F_mc / A_mc. That pressure acts on the larger caliper piston, F_clamp = p × A_cal. In the lab’s illustrative corner the whole chain multiplies foot force by about 69: 120 N at the foot makes about 33 bar and 8.3 kN of clamp.

Each pad then produces a friction force μ_pad × F_clamp, so two pads give F_f = 2 μ_pad F_clamp, acting at the effective radius r_eff where the pad force is centred. Brake torque is T = 2 μ_pad F_clamp r_eff. At the road this becomes a tyre force F_x = T / r_roll, and the deceleration of the quarter-car is a = F_x / m. That holds only while F_x stays below the tyre’s grip, μ_road × N; beyond it the wheel slips towards lock and deceleration falls to the sliding value.

Energy: a stop from speed v converts ΔKE = ½ m v² into heat, shared between disc and pads (the disc takes most of it, roughly 90 % on many designs). Treating the disc as a lumped mass, its bulk temperature rise is ΔT ≈ E / (m_disc c), with c ≈ 460 J/(kg·K) for grey cast iron. A single 80 km/h stop of a 400 kg corner (about 99 kJ) warms a 7.5 kg disc by roughly 29 K if it took all the heat; the friction surface runs much hotter for a moment because heat needs time to soak inwards. Ventilated discs pump air between their plates to shed heat between stops; fade sets in when pads or fluid overheat.

steps.title: Rolling with the pads at rest
steps.beginner: The car is rolling and the disc spins with the wheel. The pads sit a hair away from the disc, so nothing rubs and the wheel turns freely.
steps.technical: With zero line pressure, seal rollback and disc run-out hold the pads a fraction of a millimetre off the disc (drawn about 200× larger here). Residual drag at this stage would waste fuel and warm the brake, so well-maintained slide pins and seals matter.

steps.title: From pedal to pressure
steps.beginner: Pressing the pedal pushes the master-cylinder piston into the brake fluid. Fluid hardly squashes, so the push becomes pressure that reaches the caliper almost at once.
steps.technical: Foot force × pedal ratio (3.5) × servo gain (3) acts on the 22 mm master piston: p = F / A. At 120 N of foot force that is about 33 bar. Pressure rises over a short ramp (0.25 s here) as the driver presses and the pads take up their clearance.

steps.title: The floating caliper clamps both pads
steps.beginner: Fluid pushes the caliper piston, which presses the inner pad onto the disc. The caliper body slides the other way on its pins and pulls the outer pad onto the other face, so both pads squeeze equally.
steps.technical: The same pressure on a piston 6.6 times larger in area gives 6.6 times the force: F_clamp = p × A_cal ≈ 8.3 kN at 33 bar. The floating body reacts the piston force, so the outer pad sees the same clamp. Sticky slide pins break that balance and wear the inner pad faster.

steps.title: Friction makes torque; the tyre makes the stop
steps.beginner: The rubbing pads try to stop the disc turning. Because the disc is bolted to the wheel, the tyre pushes back on the road — and that push is what slows the car.
steps.technical: Two pad faces at μ = 0.4 make F_f = 2μF_clamp ≈ 6.6 kN, acting at r_eff = 0.12 m: T ≈ 800 N·m. At the 0.31 m tyre radius that is about 2.6 kN of road force on a 400 kg corner — roughly 0.66 g, within the grip of a dry road.

steps.title: Movement energy becomes heat
steps.beginner: All the energy the car had from moving is turned into heat by the rubbing. The disc warms up — that is where the car’s speed has gone.
steps.technical: Energy converted so far is exactly ½m(v₀² − v²). Taking the disc as one lumped mass, ΔT = E / (m c): about 29 K for a full stop from 80 km/h in the lab. The colour on the disc is a conceptual heat map; a real disc only glows visibly above roughly 500 °C.

steps.title: Stopped — and the heat has to go
steps.beginner: The car has stopped and the disc is warm. Between stops, air flowing through the disc’s vanes carries the heat away so the brakes are ready for the next one.
steps.technical: Stopping distance with a pressure ramp τ and steady deceleration a is d ≈ v₀²/2a + v₀τ/2 (41 m from 80 km/h here, before reaction time). Heat leaves by convection (helped by the vanes’ pumping), radiation and conduction into the hub; repeated stops with too little cooling cause fade.

keyConcepts.definition: The same pressure acting on a bigger piston gives a bigger force. The caliper piston’s area is several times the master piston’s, so the clamp force is several times the master-cylinder force.
The turning effort the pads exert on the disc: the friction of both pad faces acting at the effective radius.
The tyre can only push on the road as hard as its grip allows, so the best possible deceleration is set by the road and tyre, not by the brakes.
At a steady deceleration the car stops in a time proportional to its speed and a distance proportional to its speed squared — double the speed, four times the braking distance.
A stop converts the car’s kinetic energy into heat in the brakes. The disc’s temperature rise depends on its mass and the heat capacity of iron.
keyConcepts.equation: E = ½ m v²,   ΔT ≈ E / (m_disc c)

misconceptions.myth: Pressing harder on the brakes always stops the car faster.
misconceptions.reality: Only up to the tyre’s grip. Past that point the wheel locks and a sliding tyre grips less, so the stop gets longer and you cannot steer. ABS exists to keep you just below that limit.
The brakes stop the wheel. The tyre’s grip on the road is what slows the car, which is why tyres, road surface and load matter as much as the brakes themselves.

misconceptions.myth: The pads press the car to a halt by squeezing very hard on their own.
misconceptions.reality: The driver supplies only a small force. The pedal lever, the servo and the difference in piston areas multiply it — about 69 times in the lab’s illustrative corner.

misconceptions.myth: Brake heat is a side effect that good brakes avoid.
misconceptions.reality: Heat is the whole point: the car’s kinetic energy has to be converted into something, and friction brakes turn it into heat. Good brakes are ones that absorb and shed that heat without fading.

practicalExamples: Double your speed and the braking distance roughly quadruples, because the energy to remove grows with the square of speed.
On a long, steep descent, use a lower gear so the engine holds the car back; riding the brakes can overheat the pads and fluid until the brakes fade.
A grinding or squealing noise when braking often means the pad wear indicator is touching the disc — have the pads checked soon.
If the car pulls to one side under braking, one caliper may be sticking or one pair of pads may be contaminated.
After driving through deep water, brake gently a few times to dry the discs and pads before you need a firm stop.

quiz.prompt: A floating caliper has its only piston on the inner side of the disc. How does the outer pad get pressed onto the disc?
options: A spring in the outer pad pushes it on
The caliper body slides inwards on its pins and its fingers pull the outer pad on
Fluid pressure acts directly on the outer pad
It doesn’t — only the inner pad touches the disc
quiz.explanation: The piston pushes one way and the body reacts the other way, sliding on its guide pins, so the outer pad is clamped with the same force as the inner pad.

quiz.prompt: Each pad is clamped with 8 kN, pad friction μ is 0.4 and the effective radius is 0.12 m. What is the brake torque from both pads?
At the same steady deceleration, how does the braking distance from 100 km/h compare with the distance from 50 km/h?
quiz.explanation: d = v² / 2a, so doubling the speed multiplies the distance by four — as does the energy the brakes must turn into heat.

quiz.prompt: A stop puts 99 kJ into a 7.5 kg cast-iron disc (c ≈ 460 J/kg·K). Roughly how much does the disc’s average temperature rise?
quiz.explanation: ΔT ≈ E / (m c) = 99,000 / (7.5 × 460) ≈ 29 K. The rubbing surface briefly runs hotter, because the heat takes time to spread through the iron.

quiz.prompt: On a wet road with a grip coefficient of 0.7, what is the best deceleration the tyres can give, however hard you brake?
options: There is no limit if the brakes are strong enough
quiz.explanation: The tyre can push on the road with at most μ times the load, so a_max = μg ≈ 0.7 g. Brake harder and the wheel locks instead.
